\chapter{Unos, Unas --- The Plural of One}
\label{ch:unos-unas}
\hlchaptermodality{253}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say some of a thing, as against the thing in general.}

I can say some of a thing, as against the thing in general.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[unos · unas]{unos · unas — the plural of \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-unos-unas}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Un libro}, \emph{una casa}. And you know where they came from: Latin \emph{\textbf{unus}}, the number \textbf{one}.

Which raises a question. What could a plural of \emph{one} possibly mean?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it stops meaning one}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{unos}} \emph{libros} — some books, a few books \emph{\textbf{unas}} \emph{casas} — some houses
\end{quote}

The moment it goes plural it stops being a number and becomes a \textbf{vague quantity}: a handful, several, a few. Not one, and not counted.

English does the same trick with \emph{a} and \emph{some} and never notices, because it changes the word. Spanish keeps the word and changes only the ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now the useful part, because you already know the alternative.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Compro} \emph{\textbf{libros}}. & I buy books — books in general \\
\emph{Compro} \emph{\textbf{unos}} \emph{libros}. & I buy \textbf{some} books — a few, this once \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The bare plural you learned long ago talks about the \textbf{kind} of thing. \emph{Unos} picks out a small, unspecified number of them.

So they are not interchangeable, and the difference is one you can hear in English too — \emph{I buy books} is a habit, \emph{I buy some books} is an occasion.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un libro}, then \emph{unos libros}
  \item \emph{Compro libros}, then \emph{Compro unos libros}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{unos} mean, given that \emph{un} means one? (\textbf{Some} — a few, uncounted.)

And what does the \textbf{bare} plural mean instead? (The \textbf{kind} of thing, in general.)
\end{tcolorbox}
